Presents a Hardcore Risk = Reward where if you don't evacuate and still keep going to get extra loot and money, if you die you lose that recruit with all of its upgrades and skill points you invested. So you need to manage the recruits and be smart with your play. Its a unique fresh take on bullet hell games. The more you play the more upgrades you unlock for weapon combinations. Only problem I have with this game its not very controller friendly. And I like playing bullet hell games with a controller. For 5€ you get some hours worth of fun of this.

[h3] The Positive [/h3] One of the best steam store trailers I've ever seen, very entertaining. [h3] The Negative(s) [/h3] Trailer is misleading, you don't build your bases, only upgrade, everything is given at the start. Upgrading characters takes forever and feels super unrewarding. Must play for a long time without dying to have a stronger character, costs a lot to heal and upgrade the character. Your strongest characters are constantly on the bench because they have to spend time in order to recover. A lot of weapons share lockouts with other weapons so your weapon selection is small. You can't choose your recruits weapon or armor, just keep re-rolling wasting gold until you get something you want. Extremely bad optimization, and visual fatigue, had to look away the last 5 minutes of my match cause my screen was nothing but particles and 5 fps. Extremely bad balancing, hit scan ranged enemies, and suicide bomber mobs that are run-ruiners for literally no reason. At no point do the enemies let up, in fact the time they should (your escape) they throw harder enemies at you, such as suicide bombers, that could be rage inducing if that were to end your run when you had planned to escape. Build variety is non-existent. Game gets boring fast, I did maybe 5 runs before I always already deciding if I wanted to keep going. Audio and music is fairly forgettable, same with the graphics. Almost no settings to change, game pauses on focus loss, forced to stay in game despite the gameplay being damn near mostly afk the last 15 minutes of the run. Despite moving being a problem, you must move in order to gain scrap and boxes to sustain your next run, mixed with the visual fatigue is hard to even see any of it. There are multiple "loot" upgrades, gold, scrap, luck, all taking up spaces of your LIMITED upgrades, need to be compacted, or just something you invest into outside of the match, meta upgrades. Limited Upgrades. Moving at all is suicide due to your speed, and the enemies speed combining, cause you and the enemies to collide into each other quickly, taking damage. Re-rolling upgrades doesn't work right, had re-rolled over 5 times, and got the same items back to back when there's still upgrades I could've received. The corny Vampire Survivor trick where enemies spawn in a circle around you with a boss, wouldn't be too much of a problem if those mobs weren't SUPER bullet sponges, and will take out half of your HP if you try to run through them. I don't think the dev's tested their own game, if the performance is completely unbearable on noob difficulty, imagine a maxed out insane run. [h3] Summary [/h3] Despite all the negatives, it has potential, but as it stands it needs a LOT of work.

Imagine making a survivors/bullet heaven game which blatantly reskinned Vampire Survivor's weapon, enemy and wave design, but still manages to make the whole formula tedious, grindy and boring because of horrible design choices and "why not" decisions. - Too many different weapons are locked behind the starting weapon pool. You cannot get them during a run. This hurts build diversity and fun factor. - For some reason some weapons are put into the same "category pool" and if you pick one of them, others get locked. Even though these weapons have different functions and evolve combinations. This hurts build diversity and fun factor. - Some evolves (eg. spear) is a huge nerf to a multi projectile build, because it locks the projectiles per attack to 4. So if you have buffs, items and perks to up your projectiles to eg. 8, sucks to be you. Makes no sense. - Too many weapons have movement based aiming. I think the genre has evolved enough at this point that this type of aiming mechanic is extremely janky, clunky and tedious. There's a reason why some other games in the genre have changed these type of weapons into mouse or auto aim. You're just digging your own grave if you pick too many of these type of weapons because then your dps just tanks. And if you want to control enemies and mow them down, you need to do the janky back n forth stutter stepping. We're over that in this genre. It was ok 2-3 years ago, not anymore. - Weapon balancing and evolves are all over the place in an uninnovative and boring way. Some weapons like the aoe garlic equivalent is the strongest weapons early game when some of the best late game weapons are extremely bad until you've evolved them. There needs to be a middle ground. Starting weapon balance is all over the place too, which means some characters are just bad from the get go. If you want to make them better, you can sink in money to upgrade their starting items but then you are ruining your meta progression and ability to unlock more things. You died because your character was too weak and you didn't grind enough? Money wasted, go grind some more. - Evolve chests are random drops from elites. FatalZone is one of those games that initially appears familiar but gradually reveals far more depth than expected. On the surface, it follows the increasingly popular formula of automatic combat against endless enemy swarms, yet it quickly separates itself through strong progression systems, permanent consequences, and survival-focused decision-making. Developed by Midhard Games and published by 101XP, the game blends roguelike action with strategic resource management in a way that keeps every run tense and meaningful. Instead of feeling like a casual arcade-style survival game, FatalZone constantly pressures players to think ahead, manage risks, and decide how much danger they are willing to face for better rewards. The core combat is fast, satisfying, and highly addictive. Players control mercenaries fighting through massive zombie-infested maps while attacks fire automatically, allowing movement and positioning to become the central focus of survival. Early encounters begin simply enough, but the intensity ramps up rapidly as larger hordes flood the screen from every direction. Dodging enemies, collecting experience, evolving weapons, and creating powerful builds become increasingly important the longer a run lasts. The game captures that familiar sense of escalation that makes survivors-like titles difficult to put down, especially once abilities begin chaining together into destructive combinations capable of wiping entire crowds instantly. What truly strengthens FatalZone is the layer of long-term progression attached to every mission. Unlike many games in the genre where death simply resets a run, FatalZone introduces permanent mercenary death, which dramatically changes how players approach missions. Characters that survive multiple runs become valuable assets, and losing them can feel genuinely punishing. This mechanic creates real tension because reckless decisions carry lasting consequences. Missions are no longer just about surviving as long as possible but also about knowing when to retreat before things spiral out of control. The extraction system is one of the smartest features in the game. During missions, players gather resources needed to improve their settlement and survivors, but staying too long drastically increases the danger level. This creates a constant balancing act between greed and survival. Do you continue deeper into hostile territory for more loot, or safely evacuate while your mercenary is still alive? That decision becomes increasingly stressful during longer runs, especially when valuable characters and rare resources are at stake. This mechanic gives FatalZone a unique sense of suspense that helps distinguish it from many similar titles that rely solely on endless survival. Outside combat, the base-building and progression systems provide another strong reason to keep playing. Resources gathered during missions can be invested into upgrading the settlement, unlocking new technologies, improving survivor capabilities, and expanding future gameplay options. These upgrades feel rewarding because they provide meaningful improvements instead of minor percentage increases. Recruiting new mercenaries, improving equipment, and unlocking advanced weapons gradually create a satisfying sense of growth that keeps the overall gameplay loop engaging for long stretches of time. The variety of builds also contributes heavily to replayability. Different classes, perks, abilities, and weapon evolutions encourage experimentation across multiple runs. Some builds focus on overwhelming firepower and crowd destruction, while others lean into survivability, mobility, or status effects. Mutations add even more unpredictability to the experience. Exposure to infection can alter mercenaries in positive or negative ways, introducing random advantages and disadvantages that force players to adapt mid-run. This system reinforces the dangerous atmosphere of the world while ensuring no two sessions feel entirely identical. Atmosphere is another area where FatalZone performs surprisingly well. The game embraces a bleak post-apocalyptic tone filled with abandoned locations, ruined environments, and relentless infected enemies. While the story itself remains fairly minimal, the setting successfully creates a sense of desperation and collapse. Enemy designs are varied enough to keep combat interesting, with special infected types forcing players to constantly reposition and rethink strategies instead of simply circling hordes endlessly. Combined with solid sound design and intense combat effects, the game does a good job maintaining pressure throughout longer sessions. Visually, FatalZone may not be revolutionary, but it delivers exactly what the gameplay requires. Explosions, abilities, gunfire, and enemy swarms create chaotic but satisfying battles, especially during later stages when the screen becomes crowded with destruction. The game generally maintains clear visual readability despite the sheer number of enemies and effects appearing simultaneously. Animations are smooth, weapon effects feel impactful, and the grim aesthetic complements the survival-heavy gameplay structure effectively. That said, the game still suffers from some issues common to the genre. Repetition can eventually become noticeable during extended play sessions since the basic structure remains focused on surviving waves of enemies repeatedly. Although the progression systems help maintain engagement, players already burned out on survivors-style games may not find enough innovation to completely refresh the formula. Certain builds and weapon combinations can also feel noticeably stronger than others, reducing experimentation once players discover highly effective setups. The difficulty may also frustrate some newcomers. FatalZone expects players to learn enemy patterns, optimize builds, and make careful extraction decisions. Greedy mistakes are often punished severely, especially because permanent character death increases the stakes significantly. However, this challenge is also one of the game’s biggest strengths because it creates tension that many similar games fail to achieve. Success feels rewarding precisely because the game does not hand out victories easily. FatalZone succeeds because it combines addictive horde combat with meaningful progression and strategic survival mechanics. Instead of relying entirely on flashy combat loops, it adds genuine risk management and long-term planning that make every mission feel important. The permanent death system, extraction mechanics, and settlement upgrades all work together to create a gameplay loop that remains engaging well beyond the first few hours. While it may not completely reinvent the survivors-like genre, FatalZone introduces enough originality and strategic depth to stand out among its competitors. Players who enjoy roguelikes, zombie survival games, and progression-heavy action titles will likely find themselves hooked by its rewarding systems and constant tension. It is a brutal but satisfying experience that rewards patience, careful planning, and adaptability while delivering the chaotic combat fans of the genre expect. Rating: 7/10
